Push 'b', push 'a', pop 'a' (smallest remaining is 'c'), pop 'b', push 'c', pop 'c' -> "abc".
Push 'b', 'd', 'd', 'a', pop 'a', then pop 'd', 'd', 'b' -> "addb".

title: Robot Collisions
description:
There are `n` robots on a 1D line, each with a distinct initial position `positions[i]`, an integer health `healths[i]`, and a movement direction `directions[i]` (`'L'` for left or `'R'` for right). All robots start moving simultaneously at the same speed.

Whenever two robots meet at the same point, they collide:
- The robot with lower health is removed from the line, and the robot with higher health has its health decreased by `1` and continues moving.
- If both robots have the same health, both are removed from the line.

Return a list containing the final healths of all surviving robots in the exact order they appeared in the input (or an empty list if none survive).
constraints: All values in positions are distinct.
hints: Sort the robot indices by their starting position from left to right so collisions occur strictly between adjacent moving fronts.
Maintain a stack of indices of surviving right-moving robots; each left-moving robot collides with the top of the stack until it is destroyed or the stack becomes empty.

examples.explanation: All robots move right, so no collisions occur and healths remain [2, 17, 9, 15, 10].
Sorted by position: 2(R,15), 3(R,10), 5(L,15), 6(L,12). Robot at 5 destroys robot at 3 (becoming hp 14) then loses to robot at 2 (leaving hp 14); robot at 6 then loses to robot at 2, leaving [13].
Adjacent opposing pairs (pos 1 vs 2 with hp 10, and pos 5 vs 6 with hp 11) have equal health and destroy each other, leaving [].

title: Maximum Nesting Depth of Parentheses
description:
Given a valid parentheses string `s` (which may also contain digits and arithmetic operators `'+'`, `'-'`, `'*'`, `'/'`), return the maximum nesting depth of `s`.

The nesting depth at any position is the number of enclosing pairs of parentheses surrounding that position. If `s` contains no parentheses, its nesting depth is `0`.
constraints: s consists of digits '0'-'9', operators '+', '-', '*', '/', and parentheses '(' and ')'.
It is guaranteed that s is a valid parentheses string.
hints: Each '(' increases the current nesting depth by 1, and each ')' decreases it by 1.
Track the running depth across a single left-to-right scan and record its maximum value.

examples.explanation: The digit 8 lies inside 3 nested pairs of parentheses.
The digit 3 lies inside 3 nested pairs of parentheses.
There are no parentheses in "1+2*3", so the maximum nesting depth is 0.

title: Remove Outermost Parentheses
description:
A valid parentheses string `s` is *primitive* if it is non-empty and cannot be split into two non-empty valid parentheses strings `A + B`.

Given a valid parentheses string `s`, consider its primitive decomposition `s = P_1 + P_2 + ... + P_k`, where each `P_i` is a primitive valid parentheses string. Return `s` after removing the outermost `'('` and `')'` of every primitive string in its primitive decomposition.
constraints: s is a valid parentheses string.
hints: Track the current open-parenthesis depth as you scan s from left to right.
Include '(' only when depth > 0 before incrementing, and include ')' only when depth > 0 after decrementing.

examples.explanation: Primitive decomposition is "(()())" + "(())"; removing outer parentheses gives "()()" + "()" = "()()()".
Primitive decomposition is "()" + "()"; stripping outer parentheses leaves "".

title: Score of Parentheses
description:
Given a balanced parentheses string `s`, return the score of `s` according to the following rules:
- `"()"` has score `1`.
- `AB` has score `A + B`, where `A` and `B` are balanced parentheses strings.
- `(A)` has score `2 * A`, where `A` is a balanced parentheses string.
constraints: s is a balanced parentheses string.
hints: Use a stack where each frame stores the accumulated score at the current nesting depth.
When seeing '(', push 0 for the new depth; when seeing ')', pop inner score v and add max(2 * v, 1) to the new stack top.

examples.explanation: A single "()" has score 1.
"(())" wraps "()" (score 1), so its score is 2 * 1 = 2.

title: Reverse Substrings Between Parentheses
description:
You are given a string `s` consisting of lowercase English letters and balanced parentheses `'('` and `')'`.

Reverse the substrings enclosed inside each pair of matching parentheses, starting from the innermost pair, and remove all parentheses from the final result. Return the resulting string.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters and parentheses '(' and ')'.
All parentheses in s are guaranteed to be balanced.
hints: First match each '(' with its corresponding ')' using a stack, storing bidirectional jumps pair[open] = close and pair[close] = open.
Walk through s starting at index 0 with direction +1; whenever you hit a parenthesis, teleport to pair[i] and flip your traversal direction to achieve O(n) total time.

examples.explanation: Reversing "abcd" inside the single pair of parentheses produces "dcba".
First "love" reverses to "evol", then "uevoli" reverses to "iloveu".
Innermost "oc" -> "co", then "etco" -> "octe", then "edocteel" -> "leetcode".

title: Valid Parenthesis String With Wildcards
description:
Given a string `s` containing only three types of characters: `'('`, `')'`, and `'*'`, return `true` if `s` is valid and `false` otherwise.

The following rules define a valid string:
- Every `'('` must have a corresponding `')'` appearing after it.
- Every `')'` must have a corresponding `'('` appearing before it.
- Each `'*'` may independently be treated as a single `'('`, a single `')'`, or an empty string `""`.
hints: Maintain two stacks of indices: one for unmatched '(' characters and one for '*' wildcards.
When seeing ')', prefer popping from the '(' stack before falling back to the '*' stack; after the scan, match every remaining '(' with a '*' whose index is strictly greater.

examples.explanation: "()" is already a valid pair of parentheses.
Treating '*' as empty yields "()", which is valid.
Treating '*' as '(' yields "(())", which is valid.

title: Check If Parentheses Can Be Valid With Locks
description:
You are given a parentheses string `s` consisting of `'('` and `')'`, and a binary string `locked` of the same length:
- If `locked[i] == '1'`, you cannot change `s[i]`.
- If `locked[i] == '0'`, you may change `s[i]` to either `'('` or `')'`.

Return `true` if you can make `s` a valid parentheses string, and `false` otherwise.
hints: Any odd-length string can never be balanced. For even-length strings, unlocked positions act like wildcards that must become either '(' or ')'.

Track indices of locked '(' in one stack and unlocked positions in another; match each locked ')' against a locked '(' first, then against an unlocked index, and finally pair remaining locked '(' with later unlocked indices.

examples.explanation: Changing unlocked positions s[0] to '(', s[2] to '(', and s[4] to ')' gives "()()()", which is valid.
"()()" is already valid even with all positions unlocked.
Odd length 1 can never form a balanced parentheses string.

title: Minimum Insertions to Balance Parentheses
description:
Given a parentheses string `s` containing only `'('` and `')'`, a string is considered *balanced* under the double-close rule if:
- Every `'('` has a corresponding two consecutive `'))'` appearing after it.
- Every pair of consecutive `'))'` matches a `'('` appearing before it.

For example, `"())"`, `"())(())))"`, and `"(())())))"` are balanced, whereas `")()"`, `"(()))"`, and `"(())))"` are not.

You may insert `'('` or `')'` at any position of `s`. Return the minimum number of insertions needed to make `s` balanced.
hints: Track the count of unmatched '(' characters on an implicit stack while scanning left to right.

When encountering ')', consume a second consecutive ')' if present (otherwise insert one ')'), and match that pair with an open '(' (or insert one '(' if none are open); at the end, each remaining '(' needs two ')' insertions.

examples.explanation: The second '(' has only one matching ')', so inserting one ')' makes "(())))" balanced.
"())" already satisfies the rule with 0 insertions.
Insert '(' before the leading '))' and two ')' after the trailing '(' for 3 insertions total.

title: XML Tag Validator
description:
Given a string `code` representing an XML-like snippet, return `true` if `code` is valid according to all of the following rules, and `false` otherwise:
1. The entire `code` must be wrapped in a single valid closed tag (`<TAG_NAME>...</TAG_NAME>`), with no characters outside that outermost tag.
2. A valid `TAG_NAME` consists strictly of uppercase English letters `'A'-'Z'` and has length between `1` and `9` inclusive.
3. Every start tag `<TAG_NAME>` must be closed by a matching end tag `</TAG_NAME>` in proper LIFO nesting order.
4. Inside tags, a CDATA section has the form `<![CDATA[CDATA_CONTENT]]>`, where `CDATA_CONTENT` may contain any characters (including `<`, `>`, or unmatched tags) and terminates at the first occurrence of `]]>`. CDATA sections cannot appear outside the outer tag.
5. Any `'<'` outside a CDATA section must begin a valid start tag, a valid end tag, or a valid CDATA section.
constraints: code consists of printable ASCII characters.
hints: Scan left to right with a stack of open tag names, handling '<![CDATA[', '</', and '<' in that priority order.
Ensure that the stack never becomes empty before reaching the very end of code (otherwise there are multiple root tags or trailing text).

examples.explanation: The snippet is wrapped in a single <DIV> tag and contains valid text and matching tags.
The unmatched '<div>]>' inside the CDATA section is ignored, and the outer <DIV> tag closes cleanly.
The tags and are interleaved () rather than properly nested.

title: Evaluate Min-Max Expression
description:
Given a valid expression string `expr` composed of signed 32-bit integers and nested binary functions `min(a,b)` and `max(a,b)`, evaluate the expression and return its integer result.

The expression follows the exact grammar (with no whitespace):
- `expr := integer | "min(" expr "," expr ")" | "max(" expr "," expr ")"`

Do not use any built-in expression evaluator such as `eval()`.
constraints: expr is a valid min-max expression with no whitespace.
Every integer literal fits in a signed 32-bit integer.
hints: Use two stacks: one for pending operators ('min' or 'max') and one for evaluated integer arguments.
Whenever you encounter ')', pop the top two values and the top operator, apply min or max, and push the result back onto the value stack.

examples.explanation: min(7, -2) evaluates to -2, and max(3, -2) evaluates to 3.
A standalone integer literal evaluates directly to -42.

title: Infix to Postfix Conversion
description:
Given an array of strings `tokens` representing a valid mathematical expression in standard infix notation, convert it to Reverse Polish Notation (postfix notation) using Dijkstra's Shunting-Yard algorithm and return the resulting list of tokens.

Each token is one of:
- An operand (alphanumeric identifier or integer literal).
- A binary operator in `{"+", "-", "*", "/", "^"}`.
- A parenthesis `"("` or `")"`.

Operator precedence and associativity:
- `"^"` has highest precedence (`3`) and is **right-associative** (e.g., `a ^ b ^ c` groups as `a ^ (b ^ c)`).
- `"*"` and `"/"` have precedence (`2`) and are **left-associative**.
- `"+"` and `"-"` have lowest precedence (`1`) and are **left-associative**.
constraints: tokens represents a valid infix expression with balanced parentheses.
Every operand consists of alphanumeric characters.
hints: Append operands directly to the output list, and use an operator stack to defer operators until higher-precedence subexpressions finish.
When pushing operator op, pop operators from the stack to output while the stack top is an operator with strictly higher precedence, or equal precedence when op is left-associative (i.e., op != '^').

examples.explanation: Multiplication binds tighter than addition, yielding ["a", "b", "c", "*", "+"].
Parentheses force a + b to evaluate before multiplying by c, yielding ["a", "b", "+", "c", "*"].
Exponentiation is right-associative, so a ^ b ^ c evaluates b ^ c first: ["a", "b", "c", "^", "^"].

title: Ternary Expression Parser
description:
Given a string `expression` representing a valid nested ternary expression, evaluate it and return the result as a single-character string.

Every condition is either `'T'` (true) or `'F'` (false), every leaf value is either a single digit `'0'-'9'` or `'T'`/`'F'`, and ternary operators are **right-associative** (grouped from right to left). Each expression has the form `cond?trueExpr:falseExpr`.
constraints: expression consists only of digits '0'-'9', 'T', 'F', '?', and ':'.
expression is guaranteed to be a valid ternary expression.
hints: Because ternary expressions are right-associative, scanning from right to left ensures inner branches are evaluated before outer conditions.
Maintain a stack: skip ':', push values and '?', and whenever the stack top is '?' upon reading a condition 'T' or 'F', pop '?', pop trueVal and falseVal, and push the selected branch.

examples.explanation: Condition 'T' selects the true branch "2".
Condition 'F' skips "1" and evaluates the right branch "T?4:5", yielding "4".
Innermost "T?F:5" evaluates to "F", then outer "T?F:3" selects "F".

title: Verify Preorder Serialization
description:
One way to serialize a binary tree is to use preorder traversal: record each non-null node's integer value, and record `'#'` for every null sentinel child.

Given a string `preorder` of comma-separated values, return `true` if it is a valid preorder traversal serialization of a binary tree, and `false` otherwise, without reconstructing the tree.
constraints: preorder consists of comma-separated non-negative integers and '#' characters.
Input is guaranteed to be well-formatted with no leading, trailing, or consecutive commas.
hints: Using a stack, push each token; whenever the top three tokens are [non-'#', '#', '#'], that leaf subtree is complete and can be collapsed into a single '#'.
Repeat the collapse after every push; the serialization is valid if and only if the final stack is exactly ['#'].

examples.explanation: Every non-null node has exactly two subtrees that collapse cleanly to a single '#'.
Node 1 only has one child sentinel '#', leaving its right child missing.
After collapsing "9,#,#" into "#", an extra dangling "1" remains, which is invalid.

title: Parsing a Boolean Expression
description:
A *boolean expression* is an expression that evaluates to either `true` or `false`. It takes one of the following forms:
- `'t'` evaluates to `true`.
- `'f'` evaluates to `false`.
- `'!(subExpr)'` evaluates to the logical NOT of the inner expression `subExpr`.
- `'&(subExpr1,subExpr2,...)'` evaluates to the logical AND of one or more comma-separated inner expressions.
- `'|(subExpr1,subExpr2,...)'` evaluates to the logical OR of one or more comma-separated inner expressions.

Given a valid boolean expression string `expression`, return its boolean evaluation.
constraints: expression is guaranteed to be a valid boolean expression.
hints: Ignore commas and push operators, '(', 't', and 'f' onto a stack.
Whenever you encounter ')', pop boolean operands until '(', pop the operator just before '(', evaluate the subexpression, and push 't' or 'f' back onto the stack.

examples.explanation: |(f) evaluates to false, and &(false) evaluates to false.
|(f,f,f,t) contains at least one 't', so logical OR returns true.
&(f,t) evaluates to false, and applying logical NOT yields true.

title: Full Arithmetic Expression Evaluator
description:
Given a string `s` representing a valid mathematical expression, evaluate it and return its integer result.

The expression string contains non-negative integers, binary operators `'+'`, `'-'`, `'*'`, `'/'`, parentheses `'('` and `')'`, and spaces `' '`:
- Multiplication `'*'` and division `'/'` have higher precedence than addition `'+'` and subtraction `'-'`, and operators of equal precedence evaluate left-to-right.
- Integer division truncates toward zero (e.g., `7 / 2 = 3` and `-7 / 2 = -3`).
- Unary `'-'` may appear at the start of the expression or immediately after `'('` (e.g., `"-(2+3)"` or `"(-7)/2"`), and no two binary operators appear consecutively.
- All intermediate and final values fit in a 32-bit signed integer. Do not use any built-in expression evaluator such as `eval()`.
constraints: s is a valid expression with no division by zero.
Every intermediate value and the final answer fit in a 32-bit signed integer.
hints: Maintain a stack of additive terms for the current parenthesis level: '+' and '-' push signed terms, while '*' and '/' combine immediately with the top term.
When seeing '(', save the current term stack and pending operator onto a frame stack; when seeing ')', sum the current frame to get the parenthesized value and restore the outer frame.

title: Number of Atoms
description:
Given a string `formula` representing a valid chemical formula, return the canonical count of each atom.

Rules of the formula:
- An atomic element always starts with an uppercase English letter, followed by zero or more lowercase English letters.
- If a positive integer immediately follows an element or a closing parenthesis `')'`, it multiplies the count of that element or parenthesized group; if omitted, the multiplier is `1`.
- Return the result as a string listing all distinct elements in **lexicographical order**, each followed by its total count if that count is strictly greater than `1` (omit the count if it equals `1`).
constraints: formula consists of English letters, digits, '(', and ')'.
formula is guaranteed to be a valid chemical formula, and all final atom counts fit in a 32-bit signed integer.
hints: Maintain a stack of frequency maps where each map represents the atom counts inside one parenthesized scope.
Push an empty map on '('; on ')', parse the trailing multiplier, pop the top map, multiply all its counts, and merge them into the new top map.

examples.explanation: There are 2 H atoms and 1 O atom, sorted lexicographically as "H2O".
Mg(OH)2 contains 1 Mg, 2 O, and 2 H atoms; sorted lexicographically this gives "H2MgO2".
K4(ON(SO3)2)2 expands to 4 K, 2 N, 14 O, and 4 S -> "K4N2O14S4".

title: Min-Max Range Stack
description:
Design a stack `RangeStack` that supports standard stack operations plus retrieving the value range (`max - min`) of all elements currently in the stack in constant `O(1)` time.

Implement the `RangeStack` class:
- `RangeStack()` initializes an empty stack.
- `void push(int val)` pushes the 32-bit signed integer `val` onto the stack.
- `void pop()` removes the top element of the stack.
- `int top()` returns the top element of the stack.
- `long getRange()` returns `(long) maxVal - (long) minVal` across all elements currently in the stack.

Every operation must run in `O(1)` time.
constraints: Methods pop, top, and getRange are always called on non-empty stacks.
At most 3 * 10^4 calls will be made across all methods.
hints: Alongside each pushed value, store the running minimum and running maximum at that stack depth.
Compute max - min using 64-bit signed integers (long in Java) so extreme 32-bit bounds do not overflow.

examples.explanation: After pushing 4, 1, 9, range is 9 - 1 = 8; after popping 9, stack is [4, 1] with top 1 and range 4 - 1 = 3.
With a single element 7, max equals min so getRange returns 0.

title: Design a Stack With Increment Operation
description:
Design a bounded stack `CustomStack` that supports incrementing the bottom `k` elements in `O(1)` time.

Implement the `CustomStack` class:
- `CustomStack(int maxSize)` initializes the stack with maximum capacity `maxSize`.
- `void push(int x)` adds `x` to the top of the stack if the stack has not reached `maxSize`; otherwise does nothing.
- `int pop()` pops and returns the top of the stack, or `-1` if the stack is empty.
- `void increment(int k, int val)` increments the bottom `k` elements of the stack by `val`. If there are fewer than `k` elements in the stack, increment all elements currently in the stack.

Every operation (`push`, `pop`, and `increment`) must run in `O(1)` time.
constraints: At most 2 * 10^4 calls will be made across push, pop, and increment.
hints: Maintain a parallel lazy-increment array inc[] of the same length as the stack.
For increment(k, val), only add val to inc[min(k, size) - 1]; when popping index i, add inc[i] to the popped value and propagate inc[i] down to inc[i - 1].

examples.explanation: Pushing 1, 2, popping 2, pushing 2, 3, 4 (4 ignored as maxSize=3), incrementing bottom 5 by 100 and bottom 2 by 100 yields [201, 202, 103], popping 103, 202, 201, then -1.
Incrementing an empty stack has no effect and popping returns -1.
With maxSize=1, only the first push succeeds and receives the lazy increment before popping.

title: Middle Stack
description:
Design a stack `MiddleStack` that supports standard stack operations plus `O(1)` access and deletion of the middle element.

For a non-empty stack of size `n` indexed `0` (bottom) to `n - 1` (top), the *middle* element is defined as the element at index `(n - 1) // 2` (the lower middle when `n` is even).

Implement the `MiddleStack` class:
- `MiddleStack()` initializes an empty stack.
- `void push(int val)` pushes non-negative integer `val` onto the top of the stack.
- `int pop()` removes and returns the top element, or `-1` if the stack is empty.
- `int top()` returns the top element without removing it, or `-1` if the stack is empty.
- `int getMiddle()` returns the middle element without removing it, or `-1` if the stack is empty.
- `int popMiddle()` removes and returns the middle element, or `-1` if the stack is empty.

All operations must run in `O(1)` time.
constraints: At most 3 * 10^4 calls will be made across all methods.
hints: Split the stack into two double-ended queues: left (bottom half) and right (top half), maintaining len(left) == len(right) or len(left) == len(right) + 1.
With this invariant, the middle element is always the back of left, and the top element is the back of right (or back of left if right is empty).

examples.explanation: Stack becomes [1, 2, 3, 4]: middle is index 1 (value 2); popMiddle removes 2 leaving [1, 3, 4] with middle 3 and top 4; pop removes 4 leaving [1, 3] with middle 1.
All queries on an empty MiddleStack return -1.
Repeatedly popping the middle from [10, 20, 30] returns 20, then 10, then 30, then -1.

title: Max Stack
description:
Design a max stack data structure `MaxStack` that supports standard stack operations and also supports finding and removing the stack's maximum element.

Implement the `MaxStack` class:
- `MaxStack()` initializes the stack object.
- `void push(int x)` pushes element `x` onto the stack.
- `int pop()` removes and returns the element on top of the stack.
- `int top()` returns the element on top of the stack without removing it.
- `int peekMax()` retrieves the maximum element in the stack without removing it.
- `int popMax()` retrieves the maximum element in the stack and removes it. If there is more than one maximum element, remove only the **top-most** one.

Aim for `O(log n)` time per operation (`O(1)` amortized for `top`).
constraints: Methods pop, top, peekMax, and popMax are always called on non-empty stacks.
At most 3 * 10^4 calls will be made across all methods.
hints: Assign a strictly increasing sequence ID to every pushed element so ties in value are broken by largest ID (closest to the top).
Maintain both a regular stack and a max-heap storing (value, id), along with a set of lazily deleted IDs that are skipped whenever they surface at the top of either structure.

examples.explanation: Stack is [5, 1, 5]: top is 5, popMax removes the top-most 5 leaving [5, 1], top is 1, peekMax is 5, pop returns 1, and top is 5.
Duplicate maximums are removed from top-most to bottom-most by repeated popMax calls.
Extreme 32-bit signed integers are compared without overflow.

title: Maximum Frequency Stack
description:
Design a stack-like data structure `FreqStack` that pushes elements to the stack and pops the most frequent element from the stack.

Implement the `FreqStack` class:
- `FreqStack()` constructs an empty frequency stack.
- `void push(int val)` pushes an integer `val` onto the top of the stack.
- `int pop()` removes and returns the most frequent element in the stack. If there is a tie for the most frequent element, the element closest to the stack's top is removed and returned.

Both `push` and `pop` must run in `O(1)` time.
constraints: At most 2 * 10^4 calls will be made to push and pop.
It is guaranteed that there will be at least one element in the stack before calling pop.
hints: Maintain a frequency map freq[val] and a map of stacks group[f] storing all values pushed at frequency level f in push order.
Track maxFreq: pop always removes the top of group[maxFreq], decrements freq[val], and decrements maxFreq whenever group[maxFreq] becomes empty.

examples.explanation: After pushing [5,7,5,7,4,5], 5 has freq 3 so pop returns 5; then 5 and 7 tie at freq 2 with 7 closer to top so pop returns 7; next 5 (freq 2), then 4 (closest to top among freq 1).
When all values are distinct, FreqStack behaves identically to a standard LIFO stack.
After popping down to empty and pushing again, frequencies reset cleanly.

title: Clear Digits With Left Letters
description:
You are given a string `s` consisting of lowercase English letters and digits (`'0'`-`'9'`).

Repeatedly perform the following operation while any digit remains in `s`:
- Find the leftmost digit in `s` and delete it, together with the closest remaining non-digit character to its left (if one exists).

Return the resulting string after all digits have been removed.
constraints: s consists only of lowercase English letters and digits '0'-'9'.
hints: Process characters from left to right using a stack of surviving letters.
Push each letter onto the stack; whenever you see a digit, pop the top letter if the stack is non-empty.

examples.explanation: "abc" has no digits, so all characters remain.
Digit '3' removes 'b' (leaving "c4"), then digit '4' removes 'c', leaving "".
Digit '1' removes 'b' and digit '2' removes 'a', leaving "cd".

title: Minimum String Length After AB and CD Removals
description:
You are given a string `s` consisting only of uppercase English letters.

In one operation, you may remove any occurrence of either the substring `"AB"` or the substring `"CD"` from `s`. After a removal, the remaining left and right parts concatenate directly, which may form new `"AB"` or `"CD"` substrings.

Return the minimum possible length of the resulting string after performing any number of operations.
constraints: s consists only of uppercase English letters.
hints: Because "AB" and "CD" use disjoint pairs of characters, greedily cancelling them as soon as they meet is always optimal.
Scan left to right with a stack: pop when the stack top and current character form "AB" or "CD", otherwise push.

examples.explanation: Removing "AB" yields "FCACDB", removing "CD" yields "FCAB", and removing "AB" leaves "FC" of length 2.
No "AB" or "CD" substring can ever be formed, so length stays 5.
Inner "CD" cancels first, bringing 'A' and 'B' together so they also cancel, leaving length 0.

title: Replace Non-Coprime Numbers in Array
description:
You are given an array of positive integers `nums`. Repeatedly perform the following steps until no valid pair remains:
1. Find any two adjacent numbers in `nums` that are **non-coprime** (i.e., `gcd(x, y) > 1`).
2. Delete both numbers and replace them with their least common multiple `lcm(x, y)`.

It can be proven that the final array is identical regardless of the order in which adjacent non-coprime pairs are merged. Return the final modified array. It is guaranteed that all values in the final array are at most `10^8`.
constraints: All values in the final array are at most 10^8.
hints: Maintain a stack representing the reduced prefix of the array.
When processing x, repeatedly pop the stack top y while gcd(y, x) > 1 and set x = lcm(y, x), then push x.

examples.explanation: [6,4] merges to 12, [12,3] merges to 12, then [2,7,6] stays until [6,2] merges to 6; final array is [12,7,6].
All adjacent merges collapse [2,2,1,1,3,3,3] into [2,1,1,3].
Merging 6 and 4 gives 12, then merging 12 with 9 gives 36, and 36 with 5 is coprime.

title: Longest Absolute File Path
description:
Suppose a file system is serialized into a string `input` where entries are separated by newline characters `'\n'`, and the nesting depth of each entry is given by the number of leading tab characters `'\t'`.

- A directory name contains no period `'.'`, whereas a file name always contains at least one period `'.'` (e.g., `"file.ext"`).
- Every entry at depth `d > 0` belongs to the most recent preceding directory at depth `d - 1`.
- The absolute path of an entry joins its ancestor directories and its own name with single `'/'` separators.

Return the length of the longest absolute path to a **file** in the file system. If there are no files, return `0`.
constraints: input contains English letters, digits, spaces, '.', '_', '\n', and '\t'.
hints: Use a stack storing the cumulative path length (including trailing '/') at each active directory depth.
For each line, count leading '\t' characters to get depth, pop the stack down to that depth, and update the answer if the entry contains '.'.

examples.explanation: "dir/subdir2/file.ext" has length 20, which is longer than "dir/subdir1" (not a file).
"dir/subdir2/subsubdir2/file2.ext" has length 32.
"a" is a directory and contains no files, so the answer is 0.

title: Remove K Digits
description:
Given a non-negative integer represented as a string of digits `num` and an integer `k`, remove exactly `k` digits from `num` so that the resulting number is the **smallest possible**.

Return the resulting number as a string with no leading zeros (if all digits are removed or only zeros remain, return `"0"`).
constraints: num consists only of digits '0'-'9' and has no leading zeros except possibly "0" itself.
hints: Iterate through the digits left to right using a monotonic increasing stack: whenever the current digit is smaller than the stack top and k > 0, pop the larger digit and decrement k.
If k > 0 after processing all digits, pop the remaining k digits from the end of the stack, strip leading zeros, and return "0" if empty.

examples.explanation: Removing digits 4, 3, and 2 from "1432219" yields the smallest possible number "1219".
Removing the leading '1' from "10200" leaves "0200", which strips leading zeros to "200".
Removing all 2 digits from "10" leaves nothing, so return "0".

title: Design Text Editor With Cursor
description:
Design a text editor with a movable cursor that supports inserting, deleting, and navigating text efficiently.

Implement the `TextEditor` class:
- `TextEditor()` initializes the editor with empty text and the cursor at position `0`.
- `void addText(String text)` inserts `text` immediately to the left of the cursor; the cursor ends up right after the inserted text.
- `int deleteText(int k)` deletes up to `k` characters immediately to the left of the cursor and returns the number of characters actually deleted.
- `String cursorLeft(int k)` moves the cursor up to `k` positions to the left and returns the last `min(10, len)` characters to the left of the cursor.
- `String cursorRight(int k)` moves the cursor up to `k` positions to the right and returns the last `min(10, len)` characters to the left of the cursor.
constraints: text consists of lowercase English letters.
At most 2 * 10^4 calls in total will be made to addText, deleteText, cursorLeft, and cursorRight.
hints: Represent the buffer as two stacks (a gap buffer): leftStack holds characters before the cursor and rightStack holds characters after the cursor in reverse order.
addText pushes onto leftStack, deleteText pops from leftStack, cursorLeft moves characters from leftStack to rightStack, and cursorRight moves from rightStack to leftStack.

examples.explanation: Typing "leetcode", deleting 4 leaves "leet", adding "practice" gives "leetpractice", moving left/right and deleting updates the cursor window.
Deleting or moving past the left/right edges cleanly stops at the boundary.
When more than 10 characters exist left of the cursor, cursorLeft and cursorRight return only the 10 characters closest to the cursor.

title: Dinner Plate Stacks
description:
You have an infinite sequence of stacks arranged left-to-right at indices `0, 1, 2, ...`, where every stack has the same fixed maximum `capacity`.

Implement the `DinnerPlates` class:
- `DinnerPlates(int capacity)` initializes the object with maximum stack capacity `capacity`.
- `void push(int val)` pushes `val` onto the **leftmost** stack whose current size is strictly less than `capacity`.
- `int pop()` removes and returns the top value of the **rightmost** non-empty stack, or returns `-1` if all stacks are empty.
- `int popAtStack(int index)` removes and returns the top value of the stack at `index`, or returns `-1` if that stack is empty or does not exist.
constraints: At most 2 * 10^5 calls will be made in total to push, pop, and popAtStack.
hints: Maintain a list of stacks together with a min-heap of stack indices that currently have room below capacity.
Lazily pop empty trailing stacks on pop/popAtStack, and lazily discard stale heap indices (out-of-bounds or full) during push.

examples.explanation: Pushing 1..5 fills stacks [1,2], [3,4], [5]; popAtStack(0) returns 2 leaving space at stack 0 so push(20) goes to stack 0 and push(21) goes to stack 2.
Popping from an empty structure or an out-of-range stack index returns -1.
With capacity 1, each element occupies its own stack and popping middle stacks opens leftmost slots for subsequent pushes.

title: Car Fleet Count
description:
There are `n` cars driving along a one-lane highway toward a destination at mile `target`. Car `i` starts at mile `position[i]` and moves at constant speed `speed[i]` miles per hour.

A car cannot pass another car ahead of it; if a faster car catches up to a slower car (at or before `target`), they merge into a single **car fleet** moving at the slower car's speed.

Return the total number of distinct car fleets that arrive at `target`.
constraints: 0 <= position[i] < target and all position[i] are distinct.
hints: Sort cars in descending order of starting position so you inspect them from closest to target to farthest.
Maintain a stack of arrival times: if a trailing car's arrival time is <= the stack top, it merges into that fleet; otherwise push its arrival time as a new fleet.

examples.explanation: Cars at 10 (time 1) and 8 (time 1) meet at 12; car at 5 (time 7) and car at 3 (time 3) merge; car at 0 (time 12) arrives alone, making 3 fleets.
A single car always forms 1 fleet.
Car at 4 arrives in 48h, car at 2 arrives in 32.67h (catches car at 4), and car at 0 arrives in 25h (also catches up), yielding 1 fleet.

title: Car Fleet Collision Times
description:
There are `n` cars traveling along a single-lane road in the same direction, given as `cars[i] = [position_i, speed_i]` sorted in strictly increasing order of `position_i`.

When a car catches up to a slower car ahead of it, they collide and merge into a single fleet traveling at the slower car's speed (the slower car's speed never changes).

Return a floating-point array `answer` of length `n` where `answer[i]` is the time (in seconds) at which car `i` collides with the next car ahead of it, or `-1.0` if car `i` never collides. Answers within `10^-5` of the true value are accepted.
constraints: position_i < position_{i+1} for all valid i.
hints: Process cars from right to left while maintaining a stack of candidate cars ahead that could be the first collision target.
Pop a candidate j from the stack if speed[i] <= speed[j] (unreachable) or if j collides with another car earlier than i would reach j.

examples.explanation: Car 0 catches car 1 at t = 1.0; car 1 is slower than car 2 so it never collides; car 2 catches car 3 at t = 3.0.
Car 2 collides with car 3 at t = 1.5; car 1 catches car 2 at t = 1.0 before car 2 merges; car 0 catches the fleet at t = 2.0.
A single car has no car ahead to collide with, so it returns [-1.0].

title: Redundant Brackets Detection
description:
Given a valid mathematical expression string `s` consisting of lowercase English letters (variables), binary operators `'+'`, `'-'`, `'*'`, `'/'`, and balanced parentheses `'('` and `')'`, determine whether `s` contains any **redundant parentheses**.

A pair of matching parentheses is redundant if there is no operator (`'+'`, `'-'`, `'*'`, or `'/'`) directly enclosed within that pair (for example, `"(a)"`, `"((a+b))"`, or `"()"`). Return `true` if any redundant pair exists, and `false` otherwise.
constraints: s has balanced parentheses and contains only lowercase letters, '+', '-', '*', '/', '(', and ')'.
hints: Push characters onto a stack until you reach a closing parenthesis ')'.
Pop elements until matching '(' while checking whether at least one operator was popped; if none was found, that parenthesis pair is redundant.

examples.explanation: The outer pair around (a+b) wraps only an already-parenthesized subexpression with no operator directly inside, so it is redundant.
Each pair of parentheses directly encloses an operator ('+' or '*'), so none is redundant.
(a) encloses a single variable with no operator, so it is redundant.

title: Minimum Reversals to Balance Brackets
description:
You are given a string `s` consisting only of `'('` and `')'`.

In a single operation, you may flip any one character (`'('` becomes `')'`, or `')'` becomes `'('`). Return the minimum number of flips required to transform `s` into a valid balanced parentheses string, or return `-1` if it is impossible.
hints: An odd-length string can never be balanced, so immediately return -1.
Cancel all already-matched "()" pairs using a stack; the leftover string consists of c closing brackets followed by o opening brackets, requiring ceil(c / 2) + ceil(o / 2) flips.

examples.explanation: After cancelling matched pairs, "))((" remains; flipping one ')' and one '(' makes "()()" in 2 flips.
"((()" cancels to "((", which needs 1 flip to become "()".
Odd length 3 cannot be balanced, so return -1.

title: Longest Balanced Bracket Prefix
description:
Given a string `s` consisting of the six bracket characters `'('`, `')'`, `'['`, `']'`, `'{'`, and `'}'`, return the length of the longest **prefix** of `s` that is a valid, properly nested balanced bracket string.

If no non-empty prefix of `s` is balanced, return `0`.
hints: Track unmatched opening brackets on a stack as you scan from left to right.
Whenever a closing bracket fails to match the stack top, stop immediately because no longer prefix can recover; whenever the stack becomes empty at index i, update the best length to i + 1.

examples.explanation: The prefix "()[]{}" of length 6 is balanced, while the next character ']' cannot match anything.
The prefix "([])" of length 4 is balanced; the trailing '(' never closes.
The string begins with a closing bracket ')', so no non-empty prefix is balanced.

title: Matching Bracket Index Map
description:
Given a string `s` containing lowercase English letters and properly balanced brackets (`'('`, `')'`, `'['`, `']'`, `'{'`, `'}'`), return an integer array `ans` of length `s.length` where:
- If `s[i]` is a bracket, `ans[i]` is the 0-based index of its matching partner bracket.
- If `s[i]` is a lowercase letter, `ans[i] = -1`.
constraints: s contains lowercase English letters and properly balanced brackets '()', '[]', and '{}'.
hints: Initialize the answer array with -1 everywhere and push the index of every opening bracket onto a stack.
When encountering a closing bracket at index i, pop its partner index j from the stack and assign ans[i] = j and ans[j] = i.

examples.explanation: Bracket at 0 matches 4, bracket at 1 matches 3, and 'a' at index 2 maps to -1.
Each pair maps symmetrically to its partner's index while letters map to -1.
"abc" has no brackets, so every entry is -1.

title: Count Valid Parentheses Substrings
description:
Given a string `s` consisting only of `'('` and `')'`, return the total number of non-empty contiguous substrings of `s` that form a valid balanced parentheses string.

Because the count may exceed the 32-bit signed integer range, return the answer as a 64-bit integer (`long`).
hints: Maintain a stack of unmatched '(' indices and an array dp where dp[i] is the number of valid substrings ending at index i.
When s[i] == ')' matches a popped '(' at index j, every valid substring ending at j - 1 can be extended by s[j..i], so dp[i] = 1 + (dp[j - 1] if j > 0 else 0).

examples.explanation: "()()" contains 3 valid substrings: "()" at [0,1], "()" at [2,3], and "()()" at [0,3].
"))((" contains no valid parentheses substrings.

title: Special Binary String Rearrangement
description:
A **special binary string** is a binary string with the following two properties:
1. The number of `'0'`s equals the number of `'1'`s.
2. Every prefix of the string has at least as many `'1'`s as `'0'`s (equivalently, treating `'1'` as `'('` and `'0'` as `')'`, it is a valid balanced parentheses string).

Given a special binary string `s`, in one move you may choose two consecutive, non-empty special substrings of `s` and swap them. Return the **lexicographically largest** string obtainable after any number of moves.
constraints: s is guaranteed to be a valid special binary string.
hints: Every special binary string decomposes into a sequence of irreducible mountain blocks of the form '1' + inner + '0'.

Use a stack of child lists to iteratively optimize every nested level: on '1' push a new frame; on '0' pop the frame, sort its child blocks in descending lexicographical order, wrap them in '1'...'0', and append to the parent frame.

examples.explanation: Inside the outer '1'...'0', the two adjacent special substrings "10" and "1100" swap to produce "11100100".
"10" has only one irreducible block, so it remains "10".
Top-level blocks "10" and "1100" swap to form "110010".

title: Longest Balanced Multi-Bracket Substring
description: Given a string `s` consisting of the six bracket types `'('`, `')'`, `'['`, `']'`, `'{'`, and `'}'`, return the length of the longest contiguous substring of `s` that is validly balanced across all three bracket types.
hints: Push (bracketChar, index) pairs onto a stack initialized with a sentinel ('#', -1).
When a closing bracket matches the top opening bracket, pop it and update the answer with i - stack.top.index; if it does not match, push the closing bracket itself as a new boundary barrier.

examples.explanation: The substring "[()]" has length 4, while the mismatched ']' at index 5 breaks any longer valid span.
The substring "{[()]}[]" from index 1 to 8 has length 8.
No pair of matching brackets is validly nested in "([)]", so the answer is 0.

title: Minimum Cost to Balance Wildcard Parentheses
description:
You are given a string `s` of length `n` consisting of `'('`, `')'`, and wildcard `'?'`, along with two integer arrays `openCost` and `closeCost` of length `n`.

Every `'?'` at index `i` must be replaced by either `'('` at cost `openCost[i]` or `')'` at cost `closeCost[i]` (entries for non-`'?'` indices are `0` and unused). Return the minimum total cost to make `s` a valid balanced parentheses string, or `-1` if it is impossible.
hints: Greedily assign every '?' to ')' first while pushing (openCost[i] - closeCost[i]) into a min-heap as you scan left to right tracking the bracket balance.
Whenever balance drops below 0, pop the minimum delta from the heap to flip a prior '?' from ')' to '(' (increasing balance by 2); if the heap is empty or the final balance is non-zero, return -1.

examples.explanation: Replacing index 1 with ')' (cost 2) and index 2 with '(' (cost 3) yields "()()" for total cost 5; flipping index 1 to '(' and index 2 to ')' costs 1 + 5 = 6, so 5 is optimal.
Replacing the two '?' with '(' then ')' gives "()" at cost 4 + 3 = 7.
Starting with ')' makes balancing impossible regardless of wildcard choices, so return -1.

title: Evaluate Prefix Polish Expression
description:
You are given an array of string `tokens` representing a valid arithmetic expression in **Prefix (Polish) Notation**.

Valid operators are `'+'`, `'-'`, `'*'`, and `'/'`. Each operand is an integer (possibly negative). Division between two integers truncates toward zero (e.g., `7 / 2 = 3` and `-7 / 2 = -3`).

Evaluate the expression and return its integer result. It is guaranteed that there is no division by zero and that every intermediate and final value fits in a 32-bit signed integer.
constraints: tokens[i] is '+', '-', '*', '/', or a valid integer string.
The expression is valid and all intermediate/final values fit in a 32-bit signed integer.
hints: Scan the tokens array from right to left while maintaining a stack of operand values.
When encountering an operator, pop the top value as the left operand a and the next value as the right operand b, then push (a op b).

title: Postfix to Minimal Infix Expression
description:
Given a valid space-separated **postfix (Reverse Polish Notation)** expression `expr` consisting of single lowercase variables (`'a'`-`'z'`) and binary operators `'+'`, `'-'`, and `'*'`, convert it into an equivalent infix expression (without spaces) using the **minimum number of parentheses** needed to preserve the exact evaluation semantics.

Standard precedence and associativity rules apply:
- `'*'` has higher precedence than `'+'` and `'-'`.
- `'+'` and `'-'` have equal precedence and associate left-to-right.
- A left operand needs parentheses if and only if its root operator has strictly lower precedence than the parent operator; a right operand needs parentheses if its root operator has strictly lower precedence, or equal precedence when the parent operator is `'-'`.
constraints: Tokens are separated by single spaces; each token is a single lowercase letter 'a'-'z' or one of '+', '-', '*'.
hints: Maintain a stack where each entry stores (infixString, rootPrecedence), with variables having precedence 3, '*' having precedence 2, and '+'/'-' having precedence 1.
When popping right then left for operator op with precedence p, wrap left iff leftPrec < p and wrap right iff rightPrec < p or (rightPrec == p and op == '-').

examples.explanation: (a + b) has lower precedence than '*', so it becomes "(a+b)*c".
a - (b - c) requires parentheses on the right child because '-' is non-associative, yielding "a-(b-c)".
a + (b * c) needs no parentheses because '*' has higher precedence than '+', yielding "a+b*c".

title: Brace Expansion Expression
description:
Under a shell-like brace expansion grammar, an expression represents a set of lowercase words built from the following rules:
- A single lowercase letter `x` represents the singleton set `{"x"}`.
- A comma-separated brace group `{e1,e2,...,ek}` represents the **union** of the sets produced by `e1, e2, ..., ek`.
- Concatenating two adjacent expressions `e1e2` represents the **Cartesian product** (all string concatenations `w1 + w2` with `w1` in `e1` and `w2` in `e2`).

Given a valid brace expression string `expression`, return the **sorted list of all distinct words** represented by `expression`.
constraints: expression consists of lowercase English letters, '{', '}', and ','.
The output list contains at most 5000 distinct words.
hints: Maintain a stack of brace frames, each saving (unionSet, currentProductSet) before entering '{'.

On a letter, append it to every string in currentProductSet; on ',', merge currentProductSet into unionSet and reset currentProductSet to {""}; on '}', combine unionSet | currentProductSet with the popped frame's currentProductSet via Cartesian product.

examples.explanation: {a,b} produces {a, b} and {c,{d,e}} produces {c, d, e}; their Cartesian product is ["ac","ad","ae","bc","bd","be"].
The union of {a,z}, a{b,c} = {ab,ac}, and {ab,z} deduplicates and sorts to ["a","ab","ac","z"].
Simple concatenation with a single group yields ["prexpost","preypost"].

title: Parse Lisp Expression
description:
You are given a string `expression` representing a valid Lisp-like expression to evaluate to a single integer.

An expression can be:
- An integer literal (possibly negative).
- A variable name (starts with a lowercase letter followed by zero or more lowercase letters or digits), evaluated in the innermost enclosing lexical scope.
- `(add e1 e2)` returning `eval(e1) + eval(e2)`.
- `(mult e1 e2)` returning `eval(e1) * eval(e2)`.
- `(let v1 e1 v2 e2 ... vk ek expr)` which opens a new scope, assigns `v1 = eval(e1)`, `v2 = eval(e2)`, ..., sequentially left-to-right (so later bindings can reference earlier ones in the same `let` and shadow outer scopes), and returns `eval(expr)`.

All intermediate and final values fit in a 32-bit signed integer.
constraints: expression is a valid Lisp expression with single spaces separating tokens inside parentheses.
Every referenced variable is bound in an enclosing scope, and all values fit in a 32-bit signed integer.
hints: Maintain a stack of lexical scope maps (one dictionary per active 'let' block) and resolve variable lookups from the top of the stack downward.
Parse sequentially with a cursor index: on '(', dispatch on 'add', 'mult', or 'let'; inside 'let', check whether a token is followed by ')' (final expression) or ' ' (variable binding pair).

examples.input: expression = "(let x 2 (mult x (let x 3 y 4 (add x y))))"
examples.explanation: Outer let binds x = 2; inner let shadows x = 3 and binds y = 4, so (add x y) = 7; outer mult computes 2 * 7 = 14.
In (let x 3 x 2 x), x is first bound to 3 then rebound to 2, so the final x evaluates to 2.

examples.input: expression = "(let x 1 y 2 x (add x y) (add x y))"
examples.explanation: x = 1, y = 2, then x is updated to (add 1 2) = 3, and the final (add x y) evaluates to 3 + 2 = 5.

title: Remove Parentheses From Sign Expression
description:
Given a valid algebraic expression string `s` consisting of single lowercase variables (`'a'`-`'z'`), `'+'`, `'-'`, `'('`, and `')'` (with no spaces and no consecutive binary operators outside parentheses; unary `'-'` may appear at the start of `s` or immediately after `'('`), remove all parentheses while preserving exact mathematical equivalence by propagating outer signs.

Return the simplified parenthesization-free string with no leading `'+'` sign (for example, `"-(a-b)"` becomes `"-a+b"`, and `"-(-a)"` becomes `"a"`).
constraints: s is a valid expression of lowercase letters 'a'-'z', '+', '-', '(', and ')' with at least one variable.
hints: Maintain a stack of active sign multipliers (+1 or -1), initialized with [1], along with a local sign variable for the operator immediately preceding the next term or '('.
When seeing '(', push (stack.top * localSign) and reset localSign to +1; on ')', pop the stack; on a variable, apply effectiveSign = stack.top * localSign.

examples.explanation: The outer minus negates b and double-negates (c+d), yielding "a-b+c+d".
Negating (a-b) flips 'a' to '-a' and '-b' to '+b', giving "-a+b".
Two nested negations cancel on 'a', and leading '+' is omitted, yielding "a".

title: Evaluate Expression With Exponentiation
description:
Given a valid mathematical expression string `s` consisting of non-negative integers, binary operators `'+'`, `'-'`, `'*'`, and `'^'` (exponentiation), parentheses `'('` and `')'`, and optional spaces `' '`, evaluate `s` and return its 64-bit integer result (`long`).

Precedence and associativity rules:
- `'^'` has the highest precedence and is **right-associative** (so `2^3^2 = 2^(3^2) = 512`, and `0^0 = 1`).
- `'*'` has medium precedence and is left-associative.
- `'+'` and `'-'` have the lowest precedence and are left-associative.

All exponents are non-negative integers, and all intermediate and final values fit in a 64-bit signed integer.
constraints: s contains digits, '+', '-', '*', '^', '(', ')', and ' ' (no unary minus).
Every exponent is non-negative and every intermediate/final value fits in a 64-bit signed integer.
hints: Use Shunting-Yard with an operand value stack and an operator stack.

Before pushing a left-associative operator (+, -, *), pop and evaluate top operators with precedence >= current; before pushing right-associative '^', pop only operators with strictly greater precedence.

examples.explanation: Because '^' is right-associative, 2^3^2 evaluates as 2^(3^2) = 2^9 = 512.

title: Inverse Depth Sum of Nested List
description:
You are given a string `s` representing a valid nested list of signed integers formatted with square brackets `'['`, `']'` and commas `','` (e.g., `"[1,[4,[6]]]"`).

The **depth** of an integer is the number of bracket pairs enclosing it (outermost elements have depth `1`). Let `maxDepth` be the maximum depth among all integers present in `s` (or `0` if `s` contains no integers). The **inverse weight** of an integer at depth `d` is `maxDepth - d + 1`.

Return the sum of `value * (maxDepth - depth + 1)` over all integers in `s`.
constraints: s is a valid bracketed nested list of integers with no spaces.
All integer values are in [-10^4, 10^4], and the final sum fits in a 32-bit signed integer.
hints: Track nesting depth using a stack of '[' brackets (or depth counter) while parsing signed integers.
Use the identity sum(val * (maxDepth - d + 1)) = (maxDepth + 1) * sum(val) - sum(val * d) to compute the answer in a single pass.

examples.explanation: Integers are 1 (depth 1), 4 (depth 2), 6 (depth 3); maxDepth = 3, so inverse sum = 1*3 + 4*2 + 6*1 = 17.
Integers are 1,1 (depth 2), 2 (depth 1), 1,1 (depth 2); maxDepth = 2, so inverse sum = (1+1+1+1)*1 + 2*2 = 8.
No integers exist inside "[[]]", so the result is 0.

solutionCode.python:
class Solution:
    def inverseDepthSum(self, s: str) -> int:
        stack = []
        plain_sum = 0
        depth_sum = 0
        max_depth = 0
        i = 0
        n = len(s)
        while i < n:
            ch = s[i]
            if ch == '[':
                stack.append('[')
                i += 1
            elif ch == ']':
                stack.pop()
                i += 1
            elif ch == ',':
                i += 1
            else:
                sign = 1
                if ch == '-':
                    sign = -1
                    i += 1
                val = 0
                while i < n and s[i].isdigit():
                    val = val * 10 + (ord(s[i]) - 48)
                    i += 1
                val *= sign
                d = len(stack)
                if d > max_depth:
                    max_depth = d
                plain_sum += val
                depth_sum += val * d
        return (max_depth + 1) * plain_sum - depth_sum

title: Min Queue Using Two Stacks
description:
Design a FIFO queue `MinQueue` that supports standard queue operations plus retrieving the minimum element currently in the queue, all in **amortized `O(1)`** time using two min-stacks.

Implement the `MinQueue` class:
- `MinQueue()` initializes an empty queue.
- `void enqueue(int val)` appends `val` to the back of the queue.
- `int dequeue()` removes and returns the front element of the queue.
- `int front()` returns the front element without removing it.
- `int getMin()` returns the minimum value among all elements currently in the queue.
constraints: Methods dequeue, front, and getMin are always called on non-empty queues.
At most 5 * 10^4 calls will be made across all methods.
hints: Maintain two min-stacks: inStack stores newly enqueued items with their running min, and outStack serves front/dequeue with its own running min.

When outStack is empty during dequeue or front, pour every element from inStack into outStack while rebuilding outStack's running min; getMin() is simply the minimum of the non-empty stacks' running mins.

examples.explanation: After enqueuing 5, 2, 7, front is 5 and getMin is 2; after dequeuing 5 and 2, only 7 remains so getMin becomes 7.
When all elements are equal, dequeue and getMin consistently return that value.
Interleaving enqueues and dequeues triggers stack pours while preserving exact FIFO order and O(1) amortized minimums.

title: Min Stack With Add-All Offset
description:
Design a stack `OffsetMinStack` that supports standard stack operations, adding a constant `delta` to **every** element currently in the stack, and querying the current minimum — all in strict `O(1)` time.

Implement the `OffsetMinStack` class:
- `OffsetMinStack()` initializes an empty stack.
- `void push(int val)` pushes `val` onto the stack (prior `addAll` calls do NOT affect newly pushed values).
- `void pop()` removes the top element of the stack.
- `void addAll(int delta)` adds `delta` (which may be negative) to every element currently in the stack.
- `long top()` returns the current value of the top element.
- `long getMin()` returns the current minimum value across all elements in the stack.
constraints: Methods pop, top, and getMin are always called on non-empty stacks.
At most 5 * 10^4 calls will be made across all methods.
hints: Maintain a single 64-bit global lazy offset; addAll(delta) simply adds delta to offset in O(1).

When pushing val, store adjusted = val - offset together with the running minimum of adjusted values; since shifting all elements by offset preserves their ordering, top() = topAdj + offset and getMin() = topMinAdj + offset.

examples.explanation: Push 5, 2 -> min 2; addAll(10) shifts elements to [15, 12] -> getMin 12; push(3) gives [15, 12, 3] -> top 3, getMin 3; pop removes 3 leaving [15, 12] -> getMin 12.
Negative addAll shifts all stored elements downward without affecting future pushes.
When the stack empties and refills, the global offset continues working seamlessly.

title: Transactional Min Stack
description:
Design a min-stack `TransactionalStack` that supports nested database-style transactions (`begin`, `rollback`, `commit`) alongside `O(1)` minimum queries.

Implement the `TransactionalStack` class:
- `TransactionalStack()` initializes an empty stack with no active transaction.
- `void push(int val)` pushes `val` onto the stack.
- `int pop()` removes and returns the top element of the stack.
- `int top()` returns the top element of the stack.
- `int getMin()` returns the minimum element currently in the stack.
- `void begin()` opens a new nested transaction block.

title: Persistent Min Stack
description:
Design an immutable, versioned **Persistent Min Stack** (`PersistentMinStack`) where every `push` and `pop` leaves all previous versions intact and produces a new sequential version ID (`1, 2, 3, ...`), all in `O(1)` time and `O(1)` extra space per operation.

Implement the `PersistentMinStack` class:
- `PersistentMinStack()` initializes version `0` as an empty stack.
- `int push(int version, int val)` creates a new version equal to `version` with `val` pushed on top, and returns the new version ID.
- `int pop(int version)` creates a new version equal to `version` with its top element removed, and returns the new version ID.
- `int top(int version)` returns the top element of `version`.
- `int getMin(int version)` returns the minimum element currently in `version`.
constraints: Every version argument is a previously created version ID (0 <= version <= latestVersion).
Methods pop, top, and getMin are always called on non-empty versions.
At most 5 * 10^4 calls will be made across all methods.
hints: Represent stack nodes as persistent tree nodes storing (val, runningMin, parentNode), with node 0 as the empty sentinel.
Keep an array nodeOfVersion mapping each version ID to its head node: push creates one new child node in O(1), and pop simply maps the new version ID to parent[nodeOfVersion[version]] in O(1).

examples.explanation: v1 = [5], v2 = [5, 2] (min 2), v3 branches from v1 to [5, 8] (min 5), v4 pops v2 back to [5] (top 5, min 5).
Popping a single-element version produces an empty version that can be pushed onto again cleanly.
Multiple branches from the same ancestor version remain completely independent.

solutionCode.python:
class PersistentMinStack:
    def __init__(self):
        self.val = [0]
        self.min_val = [0]
        self.parent = [0]
        self.ver_node = [0]  # version 0 -> empty sentinel node 0

    def push(self, version: int, val: int) -> int:
        p = self.ver_node[version]
        mn = val if p == 0 or val < self.min_val[p] else self.min_val[p]
        node_id = len(self.val)
        self.val.append(val)
        self.min_val.append(mn)
        self.parent.append(p)
        self.ver_node.append(node_id)
        return len(self.ver_node) - 1

    def pop(self, version: int) -> int:
        p = self.ver_node[version]
        self.ver_node.append(self.parent[p])
        return len(self.ver_node) - 1

    def top(self, version: int) -> int:
        return self.val[self.ver_node[version]]

    def getMin(self, version: int) -> int:
        return self.min_val[self.ver_node[version]]

title: Design K Stacks in One Array
description:
Design a space-efficient data structure `KStacks` that implements `k` independent LIFO stacks (`0` through `k - 1`) sharing a single fixed-capacity pool of `capacity` slots, with every operation running in `O(1)` time.

Implement the `KStacks` class:
- `KStacks(int k, int capacity)` initializes `k` empty stacks sharing `capacity` total slots.
- `boolean push(int stackId, int val)` pushes `val` (`0 <= val <= 10^9`) onto stack `stackId` and returns `true` if a free slot is available; otherwise leaves all stacks unchanged and returns `false`.
- `int pop(int stackId)` pops and returns the top element of stack `stackId`, or returns `-1` if stack `stackId` is empty.
- `int peek(int stackId)` returns the top element of stack `stackId` without removing it, or returns `-1` if empty.
- `int size(int stackId)` returns the current number of elements in stack `stackId`.
constraints: At most 3 * 10^4 method calls will be made.
hints: Maintain three flat arrays of length `capacity`: `data` for values, `next` linking both free slots and per-stack chains, plus `top` and `sizes` of length `k` and a `freeHead` pointer.

On `push`, unlink `slot = freeHead`, advance `freeHead = next[slot]`, link `next[slot] = top[stackId]`, and set `top[stackId] = slot`; on `pop`, reverse those exact links to return the slot to the free list in O(1).

examples.explanation: With capacity 3 across 2 stacks, pushing 10 and 20 onto stack 0 and 30 onto stack 1 fills the pool; the next push returns false until a pop frees a slot.
Popping and peeking an empty stack return -1, while size returns 0.
Freed slots from stack 0 are immediately reused by stack 2 in O(1).

solutionCode.python:
class KStacks:
    def __init__(self, k: int, capacity: int):
        self.data = [0] * capacity
        self.nxt = list(range(1, capacity)) + [-1]
        self.top = [-1] * k
        self.sizes = [0] * k
        self.free_head = 0

    def push(self, stackId: int, val: int) -> bool:
        if self.free_head == -1:
            return False
        slot = self.free_head
        self.free_head = self.nxt[slot]
        self.data[slot] = val
        self.nxt[slot] = self.top[stackId]
        self.top[stackId] = slot
        self.sizes[stackId] += 1
        return True

    def pop(self, stackId: int) -> int:
        slot = self.top[stackId]
        if slot == -1:
            return -1
        self.top[stackId] = self.nxt[slot]
        self.nxt[slot] = self.free_head
        self.free_head = slot
        self.sizes[stackId] -= 1
        return self.data[slot]

    def peek(self, stackId: int) -> int:
        slot = self.top[stackId]
        return -1 if slot == -1 else self.data[slot]

    def size(self, stackId: int) -> int:
        return self.sizes[stackId]
